content: Neem oil is a type of vegetable oil that is extracted from the fruits and seeds of the neem tree, scientifically known as Azadirachta indica. This tree is an evergreen species native to the Indian subcontinent and has been introduced to various tropical regions around the world. Among the commercially available neem-based products, neem oil is considered the most significant. Neem oil typically ranges in color from light to dark brown. It has a bitter taste and a strong odor, often described as a combination of peanut and garlic scents. Its primary chemical composition includes triglycerides and a substantial amount of triterpenoid compounds, which are responsible for its characteristic bitterness. Neem oil is hydrophobic, meaning it does not mix with water. To use it in water-based applications, it must be emulsified with suitable surfactants. Additionally, neem oil contains steroids such as campesterol, beta-sitosterol, and stigmasterol, as well as a variety of triterpenoids. Among these, azadirachtin is the most well-known and extensively studied compound. The concentration of azadirachtin in neem oil can vary significantly, ranging from 300 ppm to over 2000 ppm, depending on the quality of the neem seeds used in its production. Neem oil is not used for cooking purposes. However, in India and Bangladesh, it is widely utilized in the preparation of cosmetics, including soaps, hair care products, body hygiene creams, and hand creams. It also plays a significant role in Ayurvedic, Unani, and traditional folk medicine for treating a broad spectrum of ailments. Ancient Ayurvedic texts frequently mention its use for managing skin diseases, inflammations, and fevers. In more recent times, it has been recognized for its effectiveness in treating rheumatic disorders and for its insect-repellent and insecticidal properties. Traditional Ayurvedic applications of neem include the treatment of fever, leprosy, malaria, ophthalmia, and tuberculosis. Folk remedies have employed neem oil as an anthelmintic, antifeedant, antiseptic, diuretic, emmenagogue, contraceptive, febrifuge, parasiticide, pediculocide, and insecticide. It has also been used in traditional medicine for conditions such as tetanus, urticaria, eczema, scrofula, and erysipelas. Historically, neem extracts have been administered through various routes, including oral, vaginal, and topical applications. Neem oil has a long history of use in India and surrounding regions for a wide range of therapeutic purposes. Puri (1999) provided a detailed account of the traditional uses, therapeutic indications, and pharmacological studies of neem oil in his book dedicated to the subject.
